analysis.one_liner: Ties the federal minimum wage to automatic annual cost-of-living increases.
analysis.headline: The minimum wage indexing bill was referred to a House subcommittee in February 1993 and never received a vote before the 103rd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend the Fair Labor Standards Act so the federal minimum wage rises automatically each year with the cost of living, the same way Social Security benefits are adjusted. Starting in 1994, the Secretary of Labor would apply the annual inflation adjustment to the minimum wage. The bill did not raise the minimum wage by any set amount; it would only keep whatever rate was in effect from eroding as prices rose. It was referred to committee, then to a subcommittee, and never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers paid at or near the federal minimum wage would gain steady protection against inflation: each January, their wage floor would rise by the same cost-of-living adjustment Social Security beneficiaries receive, instead of losing purchasing power between congressional pay raises. [S2] [S3]
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers paid the federal minimum wage

how_it_helps.text: It would end the pattern in which the minimum wage loses value to inflation every year between congressional pay increases, since the rate would adjust each January using the same formula that adjusts Social Security benefits.
It would make the wage floor predictable for workers and employers alike, removing the recurring political fights over whether and when to raise it.

analysis.who_pays: Employers whose payrolls include minimum-wage workers would bear automatic annual cost increases tied to inflation, without a one-time boost that Congress could time or phase in. If employers passed costs on, some prices would rise slightly. [S3]

drawbacks.text: Indexing alone would not raise the minimum wage or restore the purchasing power it had already lost; it would only freeze the existing rate against future inflation, so a worker earning a wage floor set years earlier would get no catch-up.

Once the adjustment is automatic, Congress would no longer debate or revisit the minimum wage level itself, which critics of indexing argue removes a point of democratic accountability — though supporters say that annual political fights are exactly why the wage erodes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but limited: indexing protects the minimum wage from further erosion, which matters most to the roughly low-wage workers the floor covers, and it does so through an automatic, nonpartisan formula. The cost is modest annual payroll increases for employers of minimum-wage labor. The design's main weakness is that it does nothing about past erosion, so pairing it with an upfront increase would have been the stronger bill. Still, as a safeguard against the wage floor silently shrinking every year, the value to workers outweighs the cost.

outcome.mechanism: The House sent it to committee, which passed it along to a subcommittee where it sat until the Congress ended in January 1995 — it never came up for a vote in either chamber.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 5, 1993 and referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor the same day.
On February 2, 1993, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Labor Standards, Occupational Health and Safety, where it remained with no recorded action.
The bill never received a House or Senate vote, and the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995 with the bill dead.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers of minimum-wage workers were better off, since no automatic annual wage adjustments took effect. Minimum-wage workers gained nothing, and the wage floor they earned continued to be set only by occasional acts of Congress.

for.name: Rep. George Miller
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Fair Wage Act of 1993 to index the minimum wage to inflation.

for.name: 13 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; it never advanced past a subcommittee referral.

against.name: House Committee on Education and Labor
against.role: House Committee on Education and Labor
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to a subcommittee on February 2, 1993, where it sat with no markup, no vote, and no further action through the end of the 103rd Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's entire visible support was Democratic — one sponsor and 13 cosponsors, all Democrats — and no House vote was ever taken.

industries.industry: Restaurants and other low-wage service employers
industries.note: Indexing would mean an automatic payroll cost increase every year for employers paying the minimum wage, removing their ability to let inflation quietly erode the floor between congressional pay raises. Because the bill died, they avoided this change entirely.

industries.industry: Retail and agriculture employers using minimum-wage labor
industries.note: Any employer with minimum-wage staff, from big-box chains to small farms, would face the same automatic annual increases. The bill's failure preserved the status quo, where the minimum wage stays flat until Congress acts.
